name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Friday 10 February 1984

clue.text: Think like wise men, perhaps, in the East

indicators.note: the little word in also tells you to put the wise men inside it, so it is read both as letters and as a placing

blocks.note: taken as written, then opened up to hold the wise men
the Magi are the wise men of the Nativity story; 'perhaps' flags them as one example of wise men
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A suggestion to meditate the way the Magi did when they set out from the East.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'in' does double duty: its two letters split to hold MAGI, then E follows, giving IMAGINE.
explanation.definitionFit: To imagine is to form an idea in the mind, a direct synonym of think in the sense of picture or suppose.

clue.text: Accepted model of an old school form

blocks.note: first meaning: the agreed benchmark everything else is measured against
second meaning: a grade or class in an elementary school, as the word was once used in British and Australian schools

explanation.surface: Someone describing the classic layout of a schoolroom in years gone by.
explanation.walkthrough: In older British and Australian schools pupils moved up through numbered 'standards', so the word once named a school class.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard is a recognised norm or benchmark, and was also the historical name for a class grade in primary schooling.

clue.text: Expanses of water forming secondary thoroughfares'?

blocks.note: B is the second letter or grade, as in B-movie
a direct synonym

explanation.surface: A wry observation that some lakes double as minor routes, perhaps for boats.
explanation.walkthrough: B-roads are Britain's secondary roads, ranked below A-roads; the Norfolk Broads are a network of shallow lakes in eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Broads are wide stretches of open fresh water formed where rivers spread out, best known from the Norfolk Broads.

clue.text: Spout about royal egg

indicators.note: about means moved around or turned about, so the letters that follow are shifted into a new order

blocks.note: the anagram fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone holding forth about a royal egg, perhaps a jewelled Faberge piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spout' looks like a verb meaning talk at length, but it is a noun here: a gargoyle is a carved water spout on a building.
explanation.definitionFit: A gargoyle is a grotesque carved figure that channels rainwater off a roof, so it is literally a spout.

clue.text: Broken rail has to form a bridge

indicators.note: something broken has its parts knocked out of place, so these letters need reassembling

blocks.note: the four letters of rail rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: A damaged railing being pressed into service as a makeshift crossing.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rialto is the famous stone bridge over the Grand Canal in Venice, so the answer is one particular bridge.

clue.text: Poor players from the green room, perhaps

definitions.note: a cryptic description of a herb, not a noun synonym

indicators.note: poor means badly made or in bad shape, so the word after it is reworked into a new order

blocks.note: the anagram fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Bad actors emerging from the theatre's waiting room before going on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: The green room is where actors wait offstage, so 'poor players' looks like a description of bad actors; in fact 'Poor' says to rearrange 'players', and the definition is a loose, playful hint at a herb grown in a green plot.
explanation.definitionFit: Parsley is a leafy green herb picked from a garden bed or herb patch, which the clue whimsically calls a green room.

clue.text: Claim to be right relating . to love

blocks.note: claiming to be something is saying 'I am a ...'
a Tory is on the political right

explanation.surface: A politician insists their conservative views are really about affection.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the wordplay as a boast: 'I am a Tory' is a claim to be right-wing, and AM A TORY runs together into the answer. The stray full stop is a scanning blemish.
explanation.definitionFit: Amatory is a formal adjective meaning concerned with romantic or sexual love, as in amatory verse.

clue.text: Excellent heading for financial column?

blocks.note: first meaning: first-rate, a slightly old-fashioned exclamation of approval
second meaning, a punning one: the crowning top of a column, and also money for investment

explanation.surface: An editor approving a title for the money pages of a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark warns of wordplay: in architecture the head of a pillar has a name, and that same word means funds, so one word covers both senses of 'financial column'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means first-rate as an adjective, and as a noun names both the top of a pillar and invested money.

clue.text: Tyrannical boss who worked hard on water

blocks.note: first meaning: a harsh employer who pushes staff relentlessly
second meaning, read literally: the overseer on a galley who drove the oarsmen, working them hard at sea

explanation.surface: A description of an overbearing manager who once laboured on boats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worked hard' looks like it describes the boss's own toil; in fact the boss worked others hard, as the overseer of galley slaves did.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for a demanding boss, taken from the overseers who drove enslaved labourers, including rowers on galleys.

clue.text: Grow old and become up set at what's to be done

indicators.note: to become upset is to be knocked over and thrown into disorder, so the word just before is rearranged

blocks.note: to age is to grow old
the three letters of 'and' in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone ageing and getting flustered over their list of chores.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' looks like a joining word but is the anagram fodder. The scan splits 'upset' into two words.
explanation.definitionFit: An agenda is a list of items to be dealt with, so it is literally the things to be done, from Latin agere.

clue.text: Supporter with an inclination to be one up in law

blocks.note: a leg supports a table or chair
the indefinite article as a single letter
a list is a lean or tilt, as of a ship

explanation.surface: A backer who fancies being one step ahead in a legal dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One up' suggests winning; here 'up in' means well versed in, as in 'up in the rules'.
explanation.definitionFit: A legalist is a person expert in, or strictly attached to, the letter of the law, hence one well informed about it.

clue.text: She would not be of much account in India

definitions.text: would not be of much account in India
definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for a coin, not a noun

blocks.note: first meaning: a woman's first name, so a 'she'

blocks.clueFragment: would not be of much account in India
blocks.note: second meaning: a former Indian coin worth a sixteenth of a rupee

explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints a woman of no standing in India; in fact the second half describes a small coin of low value in the old Indian currency.
explanation.definitionFit: Anna is a common girl's name, and an anna was a small Indian coin of little value, one sixteenth of a rupee.

clue.text: Superlative digs with a toy shovel?

indicators.note: the question mark signals that the toy-shovel picture is not literal and the letters must be dug over into a new order

blocks.note: the anagram fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A child digging a grand sandcastle on the beach with a little spade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digs' looks like a verb about shovelling, but it is British slang for lodgings; the Savoy is a luxury hotel on the Strand in London.
explanation.definitionFit: The Savoy is one of London's grandest hotels, so it counts as top-class lodgings, which is what 'digs' means.

clue.text: What editor heard about leader

indicators.note: about means turned around, so all the letters before it are mixed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor
taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about what a newspaper editor was told concerning a party chief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader' suggests a newspaper editorial, which fits the editor; it is a political leader instead. Edward Heath led the British Conservatives and was Prime Minister 1970-74.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Heath was British Prime Minister and Conservative Party leader, so he is an example of a leader.

clue.text: First-class leader going astray in Yorkshire

definitions.note: names where the answer is, not what it is

indicators.note: letters that go astray wander from their places, so this word is rearranged

blocks.note: A1 means first-class, with the 1 read as the letter I
the six letters of leader rearranged

explanation.surface: An excellent leader who has lost the way somewhere in the north of England.
explanation.walkthrough: Yorkshire is a large county in northern England; Airedale is the valley of the River Aire there. The definition is loose: it says where, not what.
explanation.definitionFit: Airedale is a district and dale in West Yorkshire, which also gave its name to the Airedale terrier.

clue.text: Sets a pattern at going into church

definitions.note: a verb phrase describing the noun answer

indicators.note: going into means entering, so the short word is placed inside the longer one

blocks.note: a temple is a place of worship
taken as written

explanation.surface: Churchgoing as a habit that establishes a routine.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition describes what the thing does rather than naming it: a template is what sets a pattern for copies.
explanation.definitionFit: A template is a shaped guide or master copy from which identical items are produced, so it establishes the pattern.

clue.text: Lots and lots to read

blocks.note: first meaning: great quantities
second meaning: books, things one reads

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a huge reading list; the two halves are separate meanings, a large amount and books.
explanation.definitionFit: Volumes means large quantities in idiom, and a volume is a single book, something one picks up to read.

clue.text: Seems to be right out of spare part

indicators.note: taking something out of a word means removing those letters from it
spare can mean wild or frantic, as in going spare, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: RT is a standard abbreviation for right
taken as written before the deletion

explanation.surface: Something looks correct but is missing from a replacement component.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove R and T from SPARE PART, then rearrange the seven letters left. 'Spare' does double duty as fodder and as the sign to reorder.
explanation.definitionFit: Appears and seems are direct synonyms when describing how something looks or comes across.

clue.text: Turn over rendering to a girl

indicators.note: over says one piece sits ahead of the other, so the girl's name comes first and the other piece is joined after it

blocks.note: Con is a short form of the name Constance
a rendering of a text or tune is one version of it

explanation.surface: Handing a translation over to a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn over' looks like one phrase, but 'Turn' alone is the definition and 'over' places the girl before the rendering.
explanation.definitionFit: A conversion is a change of form, use or belief, so it is a turn in the sense of a changing course.

clue.text: Gave a new face to man following adventuress

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the man's letters are placed behind the other piece rather than before it

blocks.note: a vamp is a seductive woman who exploits men, an adventuress
Ed is a man's name, used in crosswords for any man

explanation.surface: Someone gave a fresh look to a fellow who trailed after a scheming woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The man comes after the adventuress, so his letters go last.
explanation.definitionFit: To vamp is to renovate or patch up, originally by fitting a new front upper to a shoe, so it means refaced.

clue.text: Arm rising to acquire little gold, perhaps

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means read from the bottom up, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: a gun is a firearm, an arm
a direct synonym

explanation.surface: A soldier raising a weapon to grab a small piece of treasure.
explanation.definitionFit: A nugget is a small lump of naturally occurring gold; 'perhaps' allows for nuggets of other metals.

clue.text: Plans the return of a war time favourite

indicators.note: a return comes back the way it went, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: the tinned luncheon meat was a staple of rationing in the Second World War

explanation.surface: Someone scheming to bring back a much-loved food from the war years.
explanation.walkthrough: Spam was a wartime staple when fresh meat was rationed.
explanation.definitionFit: Maps and plans are both drawn layouts of an area, so a plan of a site is a kind of map.

clue.text: Tree-insect lonely Dickensian discovered

blocks.note: a gum tree, the eucalyptus
a midge is a tiny biting fly

explanation.surface: A naturalist finding a bug on a branch alongside a solitary character from Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Gummidge in David Copperfield calls herself 'a lone lorn creetur'; 'discovered' rounds off the definition, the character the wordplay brings to light.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Gummidge is the self-pitying widow in Dickens's David Copperfield, forever lamenting that she is lone and forlorn.

clue.text: Jimson as third man?

blocks.note: surface reading: a man named Jimson fielding at third man, a cricket position behind the slips on the off side
setter's reading: the third narrator of Joyce Cary's trilogy, the painter in The Horse's Mouth, whose first name is also a cricket fielding position near third man

explanation.surface: A cricketer called Jimson being posted to the deep fielding position of third man.
explanation.walkthrough: Joyce Cary's first trilogy has three narrators, and the third, in The Horse's Mouth, is the painter Gulley Jimson. Gully (also spelt gulley) is a cricket fielding position close to the slips.
explanation.definitionFit: Gulley is the first name of the third narrator in the trilogy, and gulley is a variant spelling of a cricket fielding position.

clue.text: Sets aside material at jumble sale

indicators.note: a jumble is a mixed-up heap, so the next word's letters are muddled into a new order

blocks.note: rep is a ribbed fabric used for upholstery
the four letters of sale in a new order

explanation.surface: A bargain hunter putting fabric to one side at a church jumble sale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumble sale' reads as a single thing, a sale of second-hand goods, but 'jumble' is the sign to rearrange 'sale'.
explanation.definitionFit: To repeal a law is to revoke it, which is what 'set aside' means in the legal sense.

clue.text: They take a chance on those higher up the scale

blocks.note: first meaning: people who place bets
second meaning: one's superiors in rank

explanation.surface: Gamblers backing people of higher social standing.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface links the two halves, as if punters wagered on the upper classes; they are separate senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Betters are people who wager, and 'one's betters' are those of superior rank or status.
